reading.rtitle: Before You Meet Your Private Banker
paras: A first meeting with a private bank can feel like an exam. The banker uses words like liquidity, equity and fixed income, and it is easy to nod and agree to a portfolio you do not fully understand. The best preparation is not to learn every product. It is to know your own answers before you walk in.

Start with liquidity. How much cash will the family or the business need, and when? Money that you need next year should not be in investments that are hard to sell. Then think about your risk appetite. The higher the return you expect, the more risk you must accept -- there is no exception to this rule, whatever the presentation says.

Next, ask how the portfolio is diversified. A portfolio with only equity in one country is not diversified, even if it holds fifty different companies. Bonds, cash and investments in other currencies usually make the whole portfolio more stable. The more different the investments are, the less one bad year can hurt you.

Finally, if you need a credit line, ask what collateral the bank wants and how the interest rate is calculated. Banks often offer a lower rate when you keep your investments with them. That can be a good deal, but read the conditions: the longer the commitment, the harder it is to change banks later. In short, the banker knows the products, and you know the family. The meeting works best when both sides bring what they know.

listenings.text: I have been a relationship manager at a private bank for fifteen years, and I start every first meeting with a family business in the same way. I do not talk about products. I ask two questions. The first one is about liquidity. How much cash will the family need in the next two years, and when will they need it? The second one is about risk appetite. How would they feel if the portfolio lost ten percent in one bad year? Those two answers are more important than any market forecast. The higher the return a client wants, the more risk they have to accept, and many clients only understand that when the market falls. So I write their answers down, and we build the portfolio around them. The clearer the answers are, the easier my job becomes.

When we started the joint venture here in Houston, we needed a credit line to pay our suppliers before the first payments came in. I thought the bank would only look at our sales. Instead, they asked for collateral, and they wanted to see the whole family portfolio. At first I was annoyed. Then the banker explained it in one sentence. The more collateral you offer, the lower the interest rate you pay. We used part of a bond portfolio as collateral, and the rate came down by almost one percent. The lesson for me was simple. The earlier you talk to the bank, the more options you have. If you call them when you are already short of cash, it is a very different conversation.

extra_audio.text: First, you write down how much cash the family will need, and when. Then, you decide your risk appetite before the banker shows you any product. After that, you ask how the proposed portfolio is diversified across countries and types of investment. Next, you compare the interest rate and the collateral of the credit line with another bank. Finally, you ask for the proposal in writing and take it to the family board.
